prompt: What does a design system decide, beyond a page of colours and a logo?

choices.text: Whether the store accepts the app
choices.why: An app that ignores either guide still installs and runs. The guides are not the store's rules.

choices.text: Which programming language the app is written in
choices.why: A design system says nothing about the language; Material is used from Kotlin, and from React Native too.

choices.text: How parts of a screen behave and where they go
choices.why: Right. The agreement about behaviour, which bar switches sections and where the main action sits, is the useful part, and every screen shares it.

choices.text: The exact pixel size of every screen the app will run on
choices.why: Screens come in every size; a design system names parts and roles, not one screen's pixels.

prompt: Why does each platform publish its own design system rather than leaving every app to decide?

choices.text: So that what a user learnt in one app works in the next
choices.why: Right. Every user arrives trained by the apps they used before, and an app that follows the guide inherits that.

choices.text: To make Android apps and iPhone apps look the same
choices.why: The two guides put the main action in opposite corners. Making the platforms alike is not their aim.

choices.text: Because apps that do not follow it are removed from the store
choices.why: Nothing in either guide is enforced like that; an app that ignores them still runs.

choices.text: Because the system cannot draw a control it did not design
choices.why: Apps draw their own controls all the time; the guide is about expectations, not capability.

prompt: Match each job to its Material 3 component.

pairs.left: three to five sections, on a phone
sections on a tablet, down the side

prompt: The HIG says a tab bar is for navigation, not actions. Which button breaks that rule?

choices.text: A tab that opens the planner's list of courses
choices.why: Opening a section is exactly what a tab is for.

choices.text: A tab labelled with a single word and an SF Symbol
choices.why: The HIG asks for exactly that: short labels, and symbols for the icons.

choices.text: A tab that opens the settings
choices.why: Settings is a section of the app, so a tab is a fine place for it.

choices.text: A tab that adds a session
choices.why: Right. Adding is an action, and actions belong in a toolbar; a tab only moves between sections.

prompt: A team adds a seventh top-level section to an Android phone app that uses a navigation bar. What does the documentation's range suggest?

choices.text: Keep the navigation bar; it has room for up to seven
choices.why: Seven is the rail's upper end, and the rail is for tablet or desktop layouts. The bar's range is three to five.

choices.text: The bar no longer fits; a drawer or fewer sections
choices.why: Right. Three to five is the bar's range; more sections on a phone point at a drawer, or at merging some.

choices.text: Move the sections into a tab bar
choices.why: The tab bar is the HIG's component, and it has the same job as the navigation bar.

choices.text: Add a second floating action button for the extra section
choices.why: A FAB is for the most common action, not for moving between sections.

prompt: Where does the planner's add-session action sit in the HIG version of the week screen?

choices.text: In a floating button at the bottom right
choices.why: That is Material's place for it. The HIG has no floating button.

choices.text: As a + in the toolbar, top trailing
choices.why: Right. On iOS the main action sits beside the title, in the toolbar.

choices.text: As a tab in the tab bar
choices.why: The tab bar is for moving between sections, not for actions.

choices.text: Under the last session, at the end of the list
choices.why: Then a student with a long week would have to scroll to add a session.

prompt: What happens to an iOS large title when the student scrolls the week's list?

choices.text: It stays large and fixed, like a top app bar
choices.why: It changes size as the list moves; that is what distinguishes it.

choices.text: It scrolls away with the content and does not come back
choices.why: It does come back when the list returns to the top.

choices.text: It moves into the tab bar
choices.why: The tab bar holds sections. The title stays at the top.

choices.text: It shrinks to a standard title, and returns at the top
choices.why: Right. The HIG describes that transition, which keeps the student oriented while scrolling.

prompt: Why does the planner's add-session form appear as a sheet over the week rather than as a new full screen?

choices.text: It is a short task tied to the week, which stays visible behind it
choices.why: Right. Seeing the week behind tells the student that cancelling loses nothing.

choices.text: Because the HIG forbids full screens for forms
choices.why: The lesson quotes no such rule; it uses the sheet because the task is short and tied to the week.

choices.text: Sheets load faster than screens
choices.why: Speed is not the reason given; the choice is about context.

choices.text: Android has no way to show a full screen form
choices.why: Android can show one; Material offers a bottom sheet or a dialog for a short task like this.

prompt: Which of these differ between the Material and the HIG versions of the planner's week screen? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: where the add-session action sits
choices.why: Bottom right in Material, top trailing on iOS.

choices.text: how the title behaves
choices.why: A top app bar against a large title that shrinks.

choices.text: the sessions and the week's total
choices.why: The content is identical; that part belongs to the planner.

choices.text: the brand's green
choices.why: The brand's colours are the same on both.

choices.text: the name of the bar of sections
choices.why: Navigation bar on one, tab bar on the other, in the same place.

prompt: A designer moves the planner's Android version to a tablet. What does Android's documentation change about where the sections go?

choices.text: Nothing: the navigation bar stays at the bottom at every width
choices.why: On wide screens the documentation points at a rail instead.

choices.text: They become tabs at the top of the screen, as on iPad
choices.why: That mixes the two guides; Material's answer for width is the rail.

choices.text: A navigation rail down the left edge
choices.why: Right. The rail is for tablet or desktop layouts; it holds every section, with the FAB at its top.

choices.text: They move into the floating action button's menu
choices.why: The FAB is for one action, not for sections.

prompt: How many named text styles does Material 3's default type scale define?
Why does an iOS app ask for the `.body` text style instead of 17-point San Francisco?

choices.text: So the text follows the size the user picks
choices.why: Right. Dynamic Type resizes text styles; a fixed 17 points stays 17 whatever the user chose.

choices.text: Because San Francisco is not available to third-party apps
choices.why: It is the system font and any app uses it; the HIG even links to download it.

choices.text: Because 17 points is too small for body text on an iPhone
choices.why: 17 points is exactly `.body` at the default size.

choices.text: Text styles render faster than font names
choices.why: Speed is not the point; the user's setting is.

prompt: On Android, text sizes are given in ___, a unit scaled by the user's font size preference.
What does dynamic colour do on Android 12 and later?

choices.text: Switches every app to dark mode at sunset
choices.why: That is the appearance setting, not dynamic colour.

choices.text: Forces every app to use the wallpaper's colours
choices.why: It forces nothing: an app has to ask for a dynamic scheme, and one that wants its brand's colour does not.

choices.text: Offers apps a colour scheme derived from the wallpaper
choices.why: Right. Only an app that asks gets it; the choice stays with the app.

choices.text: Changes the brand colour each time the app opens
choices.why: The scheme comes from the wallpaper, not from a random pick per launch.

prompt: The HIG asks apps not to hard-code system colour values. What is the reason it gives?

choices.text: Hard-coded colours make the app larger
choices.why: Size is not the reason; the values themselves move.

choices.text: The values change between releases
choices.why: Right. Asking by name keeps the app on whatever the system uses now, in every appearance.

choices.text: Apple's review rejects any app with a hex colour in it
choices.why: An app's own brand colours are hex values; the advice is about the system's colours.

choices.text: System colours are licensed and cannot be copied
choices.why: No licence is involved; the values change, and that is the whole reason.

prompt: A team makes the planner's dark theme by inverting every light colour. What goes wrong with the brand?

choices.text: Nothing: inverting is how both guides build their dark schemes
choices.why: Neither guide inverts; each defines a dark scheme of chosen colours.

choices.text: The app stops following the system's dark mode
choices.why: Following the system setting is a separate matter from which colours the dark set holds.

choices.text: Inverted colours are refused by Compose
choices.why: Compose takes any colours it is given; the problem is what they look like.

choices.text: The green turns into a mauve pink nobody chose
choices.why: Right. Inverting #2F6F4E gives #D090B1. A dark set must be chosen, not computed.

prompt: Match each idea to the platform's name for it.

pairs.left: text that follows the user's size on iOS
depth shown by a tone of colour

prompt: In `themes.ts`'s output, which rows carry an `=` in both appearances?

choices.text: Every row, since one file produced both themes
choices.why: One file, but the last three rows differ on purpose.

choices.text: The primary action and the sections
choices.why: Those are conventions, and they differ: FAB against toolbar, navigation bar against tab bar.

choices.text: The colours and the medium gap
choices.why: Right. Those are the brand, and they are equal on both platforms in every appearance.

choices.text: Body text alone
choices.why: Body text is the row that differs: Roboto 16sp against the system font's .body.

prompt: Why does `iosTheme` not pass the brand's body size of 16 on to iOS?

choices.text: It asks for a text style so Dynamic Type works
choices.why: Right. A fixed 16 would ignore the user's text size; `.body` follows it.

choices.text: A typing mistake that the next lesson corrects
choices.why: It is deliberate; the next lesson corrects a colour, not this.

choices.text: Because iOS measures text in dp
choices.why: iOS uses points; dp is Android's unit.

choices.text: 16 points is below Apple's minimum text size
choices.why: The HIG's minimum on iPhone is 11 points; 16 is well above it.

prompt: In the planner's tokens, how large is the medium gap, `space.m`, on either platform?
A product manager wants the planner's iPhone version to have a floating action button 'so both apps look the same'. What does the lesson's split say?

choices.text: Do it: consistency between platforms comes first
choices.why: Each user sees one phone; for them the FAB is the odd one out on iOS.

choices.text: Remove the FAB from Android too, so both match
choices.why: That breaks Android's convention to match iOS's; the lesson keeps each platform's place.

choices.text: Do it, as long as the FAB uses the brand's green
choices.why: The colour is right; the place is the problem.

choices.text: Where the action sits belongs to the platform; keep the brand in colours and words
choices.why: Right. The brand travels; the conventions follow each guide.

prompt: The planner adds a 'share my week' action used once a month. Where should it go on each platform?

choices.text: Replace the add-session FAB and the toolbar +
choices.why: Those places are for the most common action, and adding a session still is.

choices.text: Among the secondary actions in the bar at the top
choices.why: Right. A rare action goes with the bar's other actions, or into its More menu, and leaves the main action's place alone.

choices.text: A fourth tab on both
choices.why: Tabs are for sections, not actions, on both platforms.

choices.text: A second floating button on both platforms
choices.why: iOS has no floating button, and Material's FAB is for the single most common action.

prompt: A student switches their iPhone to dark mode and the planner stays light. Which guide's advice did the planner ignore?

choices.text: Use the system font through text styles
choices.why: That is about type; the appearance is a separate matter.

choices.text: Follow the systemwide appearance
choices.why: Right. Every app is expected to follow the systemwide setting; the HIG says one that does not looks broken.

choices.text: Use SF Symbols for icons
choices.why: Symbols adapt to dark mode, but they do not decide whether the app follows it.

choices.text: Keep the tab bar visible in every section
choices.why: That is about navigation, not appearance.

prompt: On iOS the brand's colour enters the theme as one ___, the colour of controls and links.
Which of these is a design token in the planner's sense?

choices.text: The rule that the tab bar stays visible
choices.why: That is a platform convention, not a value the brand chooses.

choices.text: The SwiftUI view that draws the week
choices.why: That is code that draws; a token is a decision the code reads.

choices.text: The floating action button component
choices.why: A component is a part of Material; a token is a value a component uses.

choices.text: primary: #2F6F4E
choices.why: Right. One named decision, written once, that both themes read.
